description: Just curious students taking their curiosity to the next level.
summary:
We’ve been working on something we call the Radiative Protection System, or RPS: a way to keep astronauts safe from cosmic radiation on long trips through deep space.

Today’s spacecraft mostly rely on thick, heavy shielding. The problem is that when fast, heavy cosmic ions slam into a thick wall, the wall itself can shatter into secondary particles that hurt the crew just as much. RPS takes a different approach. Instead of building a bigger wall, it steers the danger away. A compact fission microreactor powers superconducting coils around the ship, plus tiny nodes on each astronaut’s EVA suit. An onboard AI watches for incoming radiation and reshapes the magnetic fields within microseconds, bending charged particles around the vessel and the people inside it.

Nothing gets wasted, either. The ship’s outer skin catches the heat and motion energy from particles that glance off or get deflected, and turns it back into electricity stored in capacitor banks. So some of the energy that would have been a threat ends up helping to power the ship.

Why does this matter? Radiation is one of the biggest obstacles to sending people to Mars and beyond. It breaks DNA in clusters that are hard for the body to repair, and it can dull memory and thinking over time. By protecting astronauts from all of that while squeezing more out of the ship’s power supply, RPS brings long missions across the solar system much closer to being safe and sustainable.
details: By replacing heavy, passive shielding with dynamic magnetic fields, we aim to completely eliminate the hazardous nuclear fragmentation caused when heavy ions smash into traditional spacecraft hulls. This ensures that the defense system actively shields the crew rather than inadvertently generating a secondary radiation shower inside the cabin.
